summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Botswana. On 11 June 2019 the High Court unanimously declared Section 164 of the Penal Code unconstitutional in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General. The Government appealed in July 2019; the Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the appeal on 29 November 2021, writing that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." On 26 March 2026 paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164 were formally deleted from the statute book by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026, made under the Revision of the Laws Act. Only carnal knowledge of an animal remains an unnatural offence under that section.

Before June 2019 the exposure rested on Section 164(a) and (c), which criminalised sodomy whether heterosexual or homosexual, applied to both men and women, and carried a maximum of seven years' imprisonment. Prosecutions were rare. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found that police "did not target same-sex activity," and former President Festus Mogae said he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would cost him an election.

Legal gender recognition rests on two 2017 High Court rulings. In September 2017 the court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker was unreasonable and violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection of the law, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. The Government announced it would appeal, then decided against it in December and issued him an identity document reflecting his gender identity. In a parallel case heard in December 2017, transgender woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau, who had undergone gender confirmation surgery in December 2016, won a ruling that the Government must recognise her gender identity; she received a female identity card after a four-year legal battle and dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana."

The administrative route remains unsettled. In its 43rd-session Universal Periodic Review outcome in May 2023, Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendation to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition, and the review recorded that "a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced" (para 570). Botswana also declined the recommendation to repeal Penal Code Section 167, which covers same-sex conduct between women.

In June 2019 the High Court held that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation; legal commentator Carmel Rickard read this as giving LGBTQ Batswana a stronger constitutionally based argument against discrimination. The Employment Act 1982 has prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2010.

Botswana recognises no same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under local law has no route to partnership recognition, and no spousal immigration or next-of-kin status follows from it.

Documented violence against trans people is absent from the record rather than shown to be high. The U.S. State Department's 2011 report found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year, and recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people. Afrobarometer's measure of tolerance rose from 43 per cent in 2016 to 50 per cent in 2021 of respondents who would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour. Official signals are mixed: in February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power; President Ian Khama deported American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, saying "we don't want hate speech in this country"; and in November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. LEGABIBO and activists described the Government's 2019 appeal as "an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia."

Community infrastructure is legally established. The 2016 Court of Appeal ordered the registration of LEGABIBO, Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation, on freedom of association, expression and assembly grounds; it runs advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work, and maintains Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre assessed in May 2024 that implementation of these precedents across Botswana and Namibia "has not been satisfactory so far."

A draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. During June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process; the intersex provision nonetheless signals movement toward broader protection.
tangentialFactors:
The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's May 2024 assessment groups Botswana with Namibia, where court orders on registration and decriminalisation have likewise gone unimplemented; the comparison is with a neighbouring jurisdiction's enforcement record rather than with Botswana's own law.

Botswana's decriminalisation sits in a regional pattern of court-ordered rather than legislative change: the 2019 High Court ruling, the 2021 Court of Appeal affirmance and the 2026 statutory deletion were each driven by litigation, and the 2026 order was made under the Revision of the Laws Act after years of legislative inaction.

Afrobarometer's tolerance series (43 per cent in 2016, 50 per cent in 2021) measures attitudes toward a homosexual neighbour, not toward trans people, and is the only attitudinal trend in the source inventory.

outOfScopeNotes:
The status of Penal Code Section 167 after the 2019 High Court ruling is unresolved in the sources: the ruling addressed Section 164, and the 2023 Universal Periodic Review records only that Botswana declined a recommendation to repeal Section 167.

Whether an administrative gender-recognition procedure now exists is not sourced beyond the 2023 review's finding that none had been introduced.

No post-2011 data on violence against trans people in Botswana appears in the inventory; the 2011 U.S. State Department finding of no reported violence is the most recent figure available here, and no trans-specific homicide or assault rate with a denominator is recorded.

The sources do not record whether the Employment Act's sexual-orientation provision has been interpreted to cover gender identity, nor whether it has been enforced in any trans-specific complaint.

The 2011 U.S. State Department report's other findings (violence against women, prison conditions, discrimination against San people) are not trans-specific and are not carried here.
